messages.text: I opened a Sparbuch for your father in 1968
I'll put €10,000 aside for Mia. For when she's 18
That's so kind. Where should it go?
Somewhere safe. You young people know these things

steps.title: Sparbuch
steps.body: The passbook savings account: for decades, the way Germans saved. Germans still keep a big share of their money in cash and deposits. There's even a word for saving out of worry: **Angstsparen**. The question is what that safety costs over 18 years.

steps.prompt: €10,000 grows 5% a year, and every year's growth keeps growing too. How much is there after 18 years?
steps.reveal: About €24,000. Not 10,000 + 18 × 500 = €19,000: from year two on, the earlier growth also grows. That's [[compound-interest]], and it needs time more than anything.

steps.prompt: Where does Mia's €10,000 wait until she is 18? Pick one and jump ahead.

choices.label: All on Tagesgeld at 1.5%
choices.ending: €13,100, and it never fell once. But prices rose too: at 2% inflation it buys what about €9,100 buys today.

choices.label: Half Tagesgeld, half a broad global fund
choices.ending: €18,600. In year six it dipped to €10,900, half as deep as an all-in fund, and it climbed back while Mia was still small.

choices.label: All in a broad global fund
choices.ending: €24,100. But in year six it fell to €10,800, and the news was loud. This only works for money that can wait, and nothing promises the next 18 years look like the last.

steps.title: What the paths show
steps.body: Safe money never fell, but lost buying power. Invested money grew more, but fell hard on the way. Neither is free: one costs [[real-return]], the other costs calm. Simplified from real data: 1.5% interest and 5% a year are illustrations, not forecasts.

steps.prompt: Why does compound growth matter so much for Mia's money?
options: It has 18 years, and growth on growth speeds up over time
Because the bank adds a bonus for children
Because funds can't fall over 18 years
steps.explanation: Compounding is slow at first and fast later. The longer money can wait, the bigger the difference between paths. Funds can still fall in any year.

messages.text: I opened a savings book for your father in 1968
I want to give Mia €10,000. For when she is 18
That's so kind. Where should we keep it?
Somewhere safe. You know these things better

t1.body: A savings book. For many years, this is how Germans saved. Many Germans still keep a lot of money in cash and savings accounts. They even have a word for saving because you are worried: **Angstsparen**. But what does this safety cost in 18 years?

p1.prompt: €10,000 grows 5% every year. The growth also grows the next year. How much is there after 18 years? Guess.
p1.reveal: About €24,000. Each year, last year's growth grows too. This is called [[compound-interest]]. It needs a lot of time.

sc1.prompt: Where should Mia's €10,000 wait until she is 18? Choose, then see the result.

choices.label: All in the savings account at 1.5%
choices.ending: €13,100. It never went down. But prices went up too. It buys what about €9,100 buys today.

choices.label: Half savings, half a fund that holds many companies worldwide
choices.ending: €18,600. In year six it went down to €10,900. Then it grew again.

choices.label: All in a fund that holds many companies worldwide
choices.ending: €24,100. But in year six it fell to €10,800. This only works for money that can wait. The future can be different from the past.

t2.title: Nothing is free
t2.body: Safe money never went down, but it buys less. Invested money grew more, but fell on the way. One costs value ([[real-return]]), the other costs calm. The numbers are only examples.

q1.prompt: Why is growth on growth so strong for Mia's money?
options: It has 18 years, and growth on growth gets faster with time
The bank gives a bonus for children
Funds can't go down in 18 years
q1.explanation: Growth on growth is slow at first and fast later. More time means a bigger difference. Funds can still go down in any year.
